explanations.explanation: That's the twist. The message says, “Weep bitterly for him who is exiled, for he will never return to see his native land.” The dead one is done with the journey. The exiled one has to keep living far from home. I think that's a sad kind of heavy.

Sickness doesn't show up anywhere in this verse. The message says to weep bitterly for the one who is exiled. The reason it gives is that he will never return to see his native land. So the tears go to the one who's far from home.
No widow in this verse, friend. The message points the weeping at the one who is exiled. It says he will never return to see his native land. That's where the bitter tears are headed.

Right, and it's a heavy line. The LORD says Shallum, Josiah's son and king of Judah, “…will die in the place to which he was exiled; he will never see this land again.” So the trip out is one way. No return ticket.
Shallum had been king, but that's not where this verse goes. It says he will die in the place where he was exiled. He will never see this land again. The throne stays behind.

Weddings aren't on the calendar in this verse. The LORD says Shallum, Josiah's son and king of Judah, will die in the place to which he was exiled. He will never see this land again. It's a sober word, and I think this one stings.

explanations.answer: He makes them serve without pay
explanations.explanation: That's it. The woe falls on the one “…who makes his countrymen serve without pay, and fails to pay their wages…” So the workers swing the hammers and the paycheck never shows up. Not even a late one.

explanations.answer: He works them through the Sabbath
explanations.explanation: The Sabbath doesn't come up here. The woe is for the man “…who makes his countrymen serve without pay, and fails to pay their wages…” So the charge is about the paycheck, not the calendar.

explanations.answer: He forces them to fight his wars
explanations.explanation: Wars aren't part of this charge. The text says he “…makes his countrymen serve without pay, and fails to pay their wages…” These are builders, and the woe is about their pay. Nothing here sends them to a battlefield.

explanations.answer: Does it make you a king to excel in cedar
explanations.explanation: You've got it, baker. The LORD asks, “Does it make you a king to excel in cedar?” The man has windows, cedar panels and vermilion paint. The question is whether any of that is what makes a king. Nice paneling is not the same as being a good king.

explanations.answer: Who will live in all these rooms
explanations.explanation: Who will live in all those rooms never comes up, friend. The LORD's question is “Does it make you a king to excel in cedar?” (Jeremiah 22:15). Nobody asks about guests or room assignments. This man has windows, cedar panels and vermilion paint, and that's the very thing the LORD asks about.
The verse doesn't ask that one. What the LORD asks is, “Does it make you a king to excel in cedar?” The question is about kingship, not how long the house lasts. Cedar by itself doesn't make a king.
Yes, friend. The father “…took up the cause of the poor and needy, and so it went well with him.” That's what justice and righteousness looked like for him. He stood up for the people with the least.

Priests and Levites aren't named here. The text says the father “…took up the cause of the poor and needy, and so it went well with him.” Those are the people the verse names, so the priests and Levites stay out of it.

Merchants and traders don't appear in this verse. It says the father “…took up the cause of the poor and needy, and so it went well with him.” That's who he stood up for. The text doesn't list anyone else.

True. After describing the father's care for the poor and needy, the LORD asks, “Is this not what it means to know Me?” So knowing Him is tied to how a person treats people. It's not about how fancy the house is.
It's true, friend. The LORD says the father took up the cause of the poor and needy. Then He asks, “Is this not what it means to know Me?” So the father's way of living is tied to knowing Him.

That's right. The LORD says, “…your eyes and heart are set on nothing except your own dishonest gain, on shedding innocent blood, on practicing extortion and oppression.” Dishonest gain heads that list. The verse follows it with shedding innocent blood, extortion and oppression.

Land isn't the target in this verse. The LORD says his eyes and heart are set “…on nothing except your own dishonest gain…” The same verse also names shedding innocent blood, extortion and oppression. Nothing here is about winning anything back.

The nations nearby don't come up in this verse. The LORD says his eyes and heart are set “…on nothing except your own dishonest gain, on shedding innocent blood, on practicing extortion and oppression.” Pleasing the neighbors isn't on that list.

It's the other way around, friend. The LORD says of Jehoiakim, Josiah's son and king of Judah, “They will not mourn for him…” Then comes the cry “Alas, my master! Alas, his splendor!” as one they will not make for him.

False. About Jehoiakim, Josiah's son and king of Judah, the LORD says, “They will not mourn for him…” (Jeremiah 22:18). Cries like “Alas, my master! Alas, his splendor!” are ones they will not make for him. The text goes on to say he will be buried like a donkey, dragged away and thrown outside the gates of Jerusalem (Jeremiah 22:19). I think that's a heavy part, so let's take it slowly.

That's what the LORD says. “He will be buried like a donkey, dragged away and thrown outside the gates of Jerusalem.” It's a heavy picture, and the text doesn't soften it. I think it's meant to show how far from a king's farewell this is.
A beggar isn't in this verse. The LORD says Jehoiakim will be “…buried like a donkey…” He will be dragged away and thrown outside the gates of Jerusalem. It's a heavy word.

The verse doesn't say foreigner. It says, “He will be buried like a donkey, dragged away and thrown outside the gates of Jerusalem.” Nothing about a king's burial in that. It's a hard verse, and I think we can just let it be hard.

explanations.answer: All your lovers have been crushed
explanations.explanation: That's the reason. The call is to cry out “…for all your lovers have been crushed.” Lebanon, Bashan and Abarim are the places named for the crying out. The text doesn't say who the lovers are, so I'll leave that open.

explanations.answer: All your fields have been burned
explanations.explanation: Burned fields aren't mentioned. The reason given for the crying is “…for all your lovers have been crushed.” That's the whole reason in the verse. The call goes out over the high country.

explanations.answer: All your gates have been shut
explanations.explanation: Shut gates don't appear in this verse. The call says to cry out “…for all your lovers have been crushed.” That's the reason given, and Lebanon, Bashan and Abarim are the places named for the crying out.
It's actually not new at all. The LORD says, “This has been your way from youth, that you have not obeyed My voice.” From youth, friend. So this refusal goes back a long way.
False, and the LORD says it plainly. “This has been your way from youth, that you have not obeyed My voice.” So the refusal goes way back. It's a habit that was built over many years.

Yes, friend. The LORD says, “The wind will drive away all your shepherds, and your lovers will go into captivity.” The shepherds get driven away and the lovers go into captivity. After that, the text says shame and humiliation follow.
Hiding isn't the word. The verse says the lovers “…will go into captivity.” They're taken, not tucked away. Shame and humiliation come after that.
Battle isn't in this verse. The LORD says the wind will drive away all the shepherds and the lovers “…will go into captivity.” Captivity is the word for them. No swords drawn in the text.

That's the picture. The one nestled in the cedars will groan “…when pangs of anguish come upon you, agony like a woman in labor.” It's a comparison for how sharp the pain will be. The text says the groaning is coming.
A soldier isn't in this verse. The LORD compares the anguish to “…agony like a woman in labor.” That's the comparison the text gives. The one in the cedars will groan under it.
No sailor, no storm in this one. The comparison is “…agony like a woman in labor.” The pangs of anguish are what's coming. The verse stays with that picture.

It's the opposite. The LORD says that even if Coniah, Jehoiakim's son and king of Judah, were “…a signet ring on My right hand, I would pull you off.” A signet ring is worn close, and He says He would pull him off anyway. So He isn't keeping him close.

False. After swearing, “As surely as I live…” the LORD says that even if Coniah, Jehoiakim's son and king of Judah, were “…a signet ring on My right hand, I would pull you off.” A ring on the right hand sits close, and still He would pull it off. That's a strong word.

Right. The LORD says He will hand Coniah over “…to Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon and to the Chaldeans.” These are the ones who want to take his life, and he dreads them. They're named plain as day in the verse.
Egypt isn't who the LORD names here. He says He will hand Coniah over “…to Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon and to the Chaldeans.” Those are the ones who want to take his life.

Assyria isn't named in this verse. The LORD says He will hand Coniah over “…to Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon and to the Chaldeans.” They're the ones he dreads. The verse says they want to take his life.

True. The LORD says He will hurl Coniah and the mother who gave him birth “…into another land, where neither of you were born—and there you both will die.” Mother and son go together. A heavy word, and I think it's one to read slowly.
It's true, friend. The LORD says He will hurl Coniah and his mother into another land, where neither of them was born. Then He says, “…there you both will die.” It's a sober verse.

That's the one. The question asks, “Is this man Coniah a despised and shattered pot, a jar that no one wants?” A broken jar that nobody wants. The very next question asks why he and his descendants are hurled out into a land they do not know.
A bow isn't in this verse. The picture is “…a despised and shattered pot, a jar that no one wants?” It's a broken jar. That's the image the question uses.

No net in this one. The question asks whether Coniah is “…a despised and shattered pot, a jar that no one wants?” Think of a cracked jar with pieces all over the floor. That's the picture in the verse.

Yes. The LORD says, “Enroll this man as childless, a man who will not prosper in his lifetime.” Childless is how the record is to read. The same verse goes on to say that none of his descendants will prosper to sit on the throne of David or to rule again in Judah.
Servant isn't the word. The LORD says, “Enroll this man as childless…” He also says Coniah will not prosper in his lifetime. Childless is how the record is to read.
Unclean isn't in this verse. The LORD says, “Enroll this man as childless, a man who will not prosper in his lifetime.” That's the word for the record. I think it's a hard one to hear.
True. The LORD says, “None of his descendants will prosper to sit on the throne of David or to rule again in Judah.” That's about Coniah's line. David's throne is named right in the verse.
It's true, friend. The LORD says, “None of his descendants will prosper to sit on the throne of David or to rule again in Judah.” That's the word on Coniah's descendants. The verse says none.
